note: Append one entry per completed HLT load run. Temporary tracking file for the 1000 TPS push.

runs.headline: Same-J swap baseline after the reliable-layer removal
runs.detail: Deleting the reliable delivery layer, moving keccak to WASM, hand-writing the ABI and using native ECDSA took matched swaps from 3 to 249 per second. The profile went flat afterwards: no single site dominates any more.

runs.headline: Profile advertises only pinned hubs, capped at 100
runs.detail: A Hub's gossip Profile carried one row per Account and crossed the 10 KB storage leaf at ~34 accounts, halting every observing Runtime. Only pinned counterparties are advertised now, so a 100-user population no longer trips it. The run still died: a second agent was rewriting the mempool mid-run.

runs.headline: Frame delay floor of 100 ms on the Hub
runs.detail: A frame costs about the same whether it carries one transaction or a hundred, so holding frames back should be free throughput. Routes converged in 901 ms and payments flowed, then the Hub halted: batching pushed 49 prepared HTLCs into one 36 KB replay leaf against a 10 KB cap.

runs.headline: Batching walls cleared: HTLC leaves, paged manifests, duplicate collapse
runs.detail: Four faults surfaced the moment frames carried real batches: prepared HTLCs shared one 36 KB record, the manifest naming them reached 20.9 KB, and a retransmitted proposal halted the Runtime outright. First green payment run afterwards, still limited by the driver rather than the Hub.

runs.headline: Payments clear 30/s with every payment delivered
runs.detail: 32 senders offering one payment per second delivered 160 of 160 in 4.9 s. The Hub spent 34 frames on them, 4.7 payments per frame, so the ceiling is still the driver's offered rate and not the Hub.

runs.headline: Same-J swaps clear 30/s on the same commit
runs.detail: 64 users settled 160 of 160 swaps: 36.0 matched per second and 32.2 fully settled. Both workloads now hold above the 30/s mark on one Hub, and neither is Hub-limited yet.

runs.headline: 128 users saturate the stand, not the Hub
runs.detail: 64 senders offered 64 payments per second and 320 of 320 were delivered, but only at 29.1 per second while 28 of the machine's 32 cores were busy. Doubling the population did not raise throughput: one OS process per user costs about a fifth of a core just to exist.
